reference.source: Sleisenger and Fordtran's Gastrointestinal and Liver Disease
clinicalPearls: Adenomyomatosis is a benign, non-inflammatory hyperplastic change of the gallbladder wall characterised by mucosal proliferation, muscular hypertrophy, and outpouchings of epithelium into the thickened wall known as Rokitansky-Aschoff sinuses
It is classified by distribution as segmental, fundal (localised), or diffuse, with the segmental form producing a characteristic hourglass narrowing of the gallbladder
Most cases are asymptomatic and discovered incidentally on ultrasound, cross-sectional imaging, or histology after cholecystectomy performed for other reasons

The hallmark imaging finding is intramural cystic spaces (the Rokitansky-Aschoff sinuses), with comet-tail reverberation artefact on ultrasound from cholesterol crystals within them and a pearl-necklace appearance on MRCP
It frequently coexists with gallstones and chronic cholecystitis, which may account for symptoms attributed to the adenomyomatosis itself
The principal clinical challenge is distinguishing focal or segmental adenomyomatosis from gallbladder carcinoma, particularly when there is asymmetrical wall thickening
Asymptomatic, confidently benign disease can be managed conservatively with surveillance, whereas cholecystectomy is appropriate for symptomatic disease or when malignancy cannot be excluded
MRI with MRCP is the most useful problem-solving investigation when ultrasound leaves diagnostic uncertainty about wall thickening
reference.pathophysiology: Adenomyomatosis results from acquired hyperplasia of the gallbladder wall in which the surface epithelium proliferates and invaginates into a hypertrophied muscularis, forming the intramural epithelial-lined diverticula termed Rokitansky-Aschoff sinuses. Chronically raised intraluminal pressure, thought to relate to gallbladder dysmotility and functional or mechanical outflow obstruction, is believed to drive both the muscular hypertrophy and the herniation of mucosa into and through the muscle layer. Bile stagnating within the sinuses becomes concentrated and supersaturated, favouring precipitation of cholesterol crystals and small calculi within them; these crystalline deposits generate the comet-tail artefact seen on ultrasound. The overall process is a reactive, proliferative but benign remodelling of the wall rather than a neoplastic or infective one, although the associated stasis and coexisting gallstones contribute to chronic inflammation. In the segmental form, circumferential muscular hypertrophy creates a stricture-like waist that can trap debris in the fundal compartment and further promote stasis.
additionalDifferentials: Gallbladder carcinoma, especially with focal or segmental wall thickening
Gallbladder cholesterol polyp or adenomatous polyp
Acute cholecystitis with oedematous wall thickening
Secondary wall thickening from hepatitis, heart failure, or hypoalbuminaemia
additionalInvestigations: Abdominal ultrasound seeking intramural cystic spaces and comet-tail reverberation artefact
MRI with MRCP demonstrating the pearl-necklace sign of Rokitansky-Aschoff sinuses
Contrast-enhanced CT to assess wall thickening and help exclude malignancy
Contrast-enhanced or high-resolution ultrasound to characterise indeterminate focal thickening
Liver biochemistry to evaluate coexisting biliary or hepatic disease
Histological examination of the cholecystectomy specimen for definitive diagnosis
redFlags: Asymmetric or focal wall thickening with disrupted wall layers suggesting carcinoma
Rapidly enlarging lesion or an associated soft-tissue mass
New or worsening jaundice or biliary obstruction
Regional lymphadenopathy or hepatic invasion on imaging
Constitutional symptoms such as weight loss and anorexia
reference.prognosis: Adenomyomatosis is a benign condition with an excellent prognosis, and asymptomatic disease requires no treatment beyond confident diagnosis; symptomatic patients are cured by cholecystectomy, and although an association with malignancy is debated the lesion itself is not reliably premalignant.
pitfalls: Overcalling focal or segmental adenomyomatosis as gallbladder carcinoma, or the reverse, leading to inappropriate management
Attributing biliary symptoms to adenomyomatosis when coexisting gallstones or chronic cholecystitis are responsible
Failing to use MRI or MRCP to characterise indeterminate wall thickening seen on ultrasound
Assuming diffuse wall thickening is always benign without considering diffuse infiltrating carcinoma
Neglecting histological review of the resected gallbladder, which provides the definitive diagnosis
references: Sleisenger and Fordtran's Gastrointestinal and Liver Disease
Blumgart's Surgery of the Liver, Biliary Tract and Pancreas
management: Reassurance and no intervention for confidently diagnosed asymptomatic adenomyomatosis
Cholecystectomy, usually laparoscopic, for symptomatic disease or where malignancy cannot be confidently excluded
Careful imaging characterisation, including MRI with MRCP for the pearl-necklace sign, to distinguish focal or segmental disease from gallbladder carcinoma
Interval imaging surveillance of indeterminate focal wall thickening where malignancy has not been confidently excluded
Management of coexisting gallstones and chronic cholecystitis, which often account for attributed symptoms
Referral to hepatobiliary surgery for symptomatic or indeterminate lesions
